Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Rohan Patel, a 32‑year‑old South Asian housekeeper, lives with his wife Maya in a two‑story apartment in Brooklyn. He has worked for the same cleaning company for five years, moving from one client’s home to another each day. Last fall, a mugging on a narrow back alley in the borough changed the rhythm of his life. He had stepped out of the parking lot of his building to grab his keys when a masked figure leapt from a doorway, shoved his arm and yanked the wallet from his pocket. The assailant’s fist struck the back of his head, and a cold spray of his own blood filled the space between them before the attacker fled into the night. Rohan was left with a fractured wrist, a bruised knee, and a sudden, unshakable sense that the street had turned hostile. When the memory of that night rises, Rohan feels the same physical ache in his wrist and the pressure behind his eyes that marked the original assault. He describes the pain as a sharp, jarring thud that mirrors the moment the assailant’s palm landed on his head. The recollection is vivid, almost cinematic: the glint of a cheap streetlamp, the sound of the attacker’s shout, the feel of the cold air as the assailant slipped away. He knows what happened but cannot find words that capture the terror. The narrative stays locked in his mind, a loop of sights and sounds that refuses to dissipate. Since the incident, Rohan has come to distrust the people he once considered friendly. In conversations with Maya, he often comments that “the world feels dangerous, not because of any particular person, but because everyone could be the next threat.” He watches others on the street with a wary gaze, his shoulders tense, his breath shallow. The belief that “people can’t be trusted” has taken root in his thoughts, coloring his everyday interactions. He finds himself questioning the safety of the building he lives in and doubting the intentions of the neighbors he has known for years. His trust in strangers has been replaced by an almost constant state of alertness. The sense that the world is perilous has intensified the memories of that night. Rohan’s belief that any passerby could pose a danger keeps his mind on edge, making it difficult to relax even for a moment. When a memory of the mugging surfaces, the anxiety it generates amplifies the physical pain that accompanies the recollection. He feels as though the world’s threat is not only external but is also reflected in his own body. Each intrusive image is not merely a replay; it is a live reminder that danger still lurks, reinforcing the belief that people are unpredictable and that the world remains dangerous. Conversely, the vivid memory of the assault feeds back into Rohan’s negative appraisal of others. The sharpness of the attack—his body’s reaction, the sudden loss of control—makes it impossible for him to see anyone else as safe. Every time he recalls the assailant’s silhouette or the motion of the wrist that was struck, he is transported back to that night’s terror. The memory serves as a constant source of proof that strangers can be violent, solidifying his conviction that trust is a luxury he can no longer afford. This reciprocal loop between memory and belief keeps him in a state of hypervigilance, making everyday tasks feel fraught with risk. Rohan’s increased vigilance has reshaped his work routine. He now refuses to travel to client sites after sunset, citing a fear of being attacked again. The cleaning company’s schedule, which once required him to work evening shifts, has become an obstacle. He has missed several assignments, and his supervisor has expressed concern about his reliability. At home, Maya senses the strain. Rohan withdraws to his bedroom after dark, avoiding conversations that might bring outside noise or activity. Their once lively evenings have given way to quiet, silent rooms, each of them feeling the weight of unspoken anxiety. The culmination of these shifts has driven Rohan to seek help. He reports feeling trapped, as if the memory of that night and the distrust he now harbors are controlling his life. He worries that the physical pain that accompanies each recollection will not subside, and he fears that his perception of the world will never normalize. Rohan hopes that therapy can break the cycle that keeps him on edge, ease the pain that echoes in his body, and restore his sense of safety so that he can once again trust the people around him.
